newsitem.title: THAILAND: THAILAND SAYS NEEDS AT LEAST $10 BILLION IN CREDIT.
newsitem.headline: THAILAND SAYS NEEDS AT LEAST $10 BILLION IN CREDIT.

text.p: Thai Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya on Sunday left cap in hand for Tokyo, saying he needed at least $10 billion in standby credit from the IMF and other lenders to ease the country's financial crisis.

A senior finance ministry source said the International Monetary Fund board was likely to consider the Thai package on August 21 after discussions among donor countries and institutions on Monday, and a signing on August 15.
"I don't know how much we will get, but we will need at least $10 billion in standby credit," he told reporters before boarding a plane for Tokyo.
He declined to elaborate and did not indicate whether the figure covered the overall package or part of it.
Thailand is seeking both technical and financial support from the IMF to rescue the country from its worst economic crisis.
Thailand's economic bubble burst after a prolonged boom which saw over-borrowing from overseas and misallocation of financial resources to non-productive sectors.
Thanong said China and Australia may join other regional countries in the talks.

"Most of the discussions will be held with countries in this region -- ASEAN, Japan and I heard possibly Australia and China," he said, adding that the programme in Japan was arranged by the IMF and not by Thailand.
Thailand is a member of the Association of South East Nations (ASEAN), which also groups the Philippines, Indonesia, Singapore, Vietnam, Brunei, Burma, Laos and Malaysia.
Finance ministry sources said only Singapore was a likely lender from ASEAN.

Other sources said Thailand was likely to borrow between $12-$15 billion with $7 billion from Japan's Export-Import Bank, $4 billion from the IMF, $1 billion from the World Bank, and another $1 billion from the Asia Development Bank, and the rest from other sources.
They said the United States could also support the IMF package once a recovery programme was worked out.
A Thanong aide told Reuters that the finance minister may meet leading figures of Japan's private sector on Tuesday before returning to Thailand on August 12.
Thailand's overall foreign currency debt is estimated by the private sector to be around $90 billion, more than 40 percent of which is short-term.

The problem has been exacerbated by a crisis of confidence which has left foreign creditors and investors reluctant to pour in much-needed funds which has subsequently caused severe liquidity problems.
In a move to win the IMF financial package, Thailand last week launched several fiscal and monetary measures to put the country back on track.

The government vowed to balance the budget, maintain at least $25 billion in foreign reserves, resolve financial sector ills, cut government risk exposure to the financial sector, maintain tight monetary policy and cap annual inflation at eight to nine perent.
